title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Frederick Douglass

sections.title: PREFACE
sections.routing_description: Garrison recalls Douglass's first antislavery speech at Nantucket, endorses his narrative, and challenges readers to oppose slavery and the laws shielding its violence.

sections.title: LETTER FROM WENDELL PHILLIPS, ESQ.
sections.routing_description: Phillips praises Douglass's testimony, invokes the fable of the lions writing history, and warns that publishing his identity exposes him to recapture under Northern law.

sections.title: FREDERICK DOUGLASS.
sections.routing_description: An editorial biography traces Douglass's life from enslavement and escape through marriage, abolitionist speaking, Civil War recruitment, public appointments, and his death in 1895.

sections.title: CHAPTER I
sections.routing_description: Douglass describes his uncertain age and parentage, separation from his mother Harriet Bailey, and witnessing Captain Anthony's brutal whipping of Aunt Hester.

sections.title: CHAPTER II
sections.routing_description: Douglass describes Colonel Lloyd's plantation, food and clothing allowances, overseers Severe and Hopkins, and the sorrow expressed in songs about the Great House Farm.
retrieval_cues: sing most when they are most unhappy

sections.title: CHAPTER III
sections.routing_description: Douglass recounts punishments over Lloyd's garden and horses, a man's sale for speaking honestly about his master, and quarrels among enslaved people over their owners' status.
retrieval_cues: still tongue makes a wise head

sections.title: CHAPTER IV
sections.routing_description: Douglass describes Austin Gore's murder of Demby and other killings of enslaved people, showing how barred testimony and unserved warrants let perpetrators escape punishment.

sections.title: CHAPTER V
sections.routing_description: Douglass recalls childhood hunger and cold, his joyful preparations to leave the plantation for Baltimore, and the kind welcome from Sophia Auld as he becomes Thomas's caretaker.

sections.title: CHAPTER VI
sections.routing_description: Mrs. Auld begins teaching Douglass to read until her husband forbids it, revealing literacy's threat to slavery. Douglass contrasts city conditions with the Hamiltons' abuse of Henrietta and Mary.

sections.title: CHAPTER VII
sections.routing_description: Douglass trades bread for reading lessons, studies The Columbian Orator, learns the meaning of abolition, and develops escape hopes while teaching himself to write from shipyard marks and copybooks.

sections.title: CHAPTER VIII
sections.routing_description: Douglass returns for an estate valuation among livestock, escapes Andrew's ownership, condemns the abandonment of his grandmother, and is sent from Baltimore to Thomas Auld at St. Michael's.

sections.title: CHAPTER IX
sections.routing_description: Douglass describes hunger under Thomas Auld, increased cruelty after Auld's religious conversion, the destruction of a Sabbath school, Henny's abuse, and being hired to Edward Covey for breaking.

sections.title: CHAPTER X
sections.routing_description: Douglass describes Covey's violence and surveillance, his own resistance after seeking protection and receiving Sandy's root, and the confidence restored by their fight. At Freeland's he teaches reading and plans an escape with fellow slaves, but they are arrested. Returned to Baltimore, he survives a shipyard assault, learns calking, and must surrender his wages to Hugh.

sections.title: CHAPTER XI
sections.routing_description: Douglass explains why he withholds escape details, describes hiring his time and reaching New York, and recounts Ruggles's help, marriage to Anna, and settlement in New Bedford. He adopts the name Douglass, finds paid work despite discrimination, reads the Liberator, and begins public antislavery speaking at Nantucket.

sections.title: APPENDIX
sections.routing_description: Douglass distinguishes the Christianity of Christ from slaveholding religion, condemns churches' complicity in enslavement, quotes a poem and Scripture, and introduces a parody of religious hypocrisy.

sections.title: A PARODY
sections.routing_description: A satirical poem contrasts professions of heavenly union with whipping, selling, and starving enslaved people. Douglass closes with a renewed antislavery pledge and his April 28, 1845 dateline.
